A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same LaCy research. Their main text, equations, figures, tables and included appendices are readable and reliably matchable across the expansion and renumbering.

before.justification: v1 reports original model-training experiments, factuality and fact-leakage evaluations, NLU results, and ablations in the main text and Appendix C.

after.justification: v3 retains these original results and adds annotation-quality measurements, call-budget experiments and inference-only delegation evaluations.

M1.justification: The core LaCy architecture, training objective and delegation procedure remain unchanged. Appendix E.5.3 adds i-LaCy, an inference-only adaptation that applies spaCy to predicted tokens and routes using negative log probability or top-20-token entropy, without modifying pretraining.

E1.justification: Appendix C adds a small factual-token annotation evaluation against human labels on two existing training documents, Burke Marshall and Jaguar XF. This extends evaluation to annotation agreement within the existing Wikipedia domain. Training corpora and biography, factual-QA and NLU benchmark coverage remain unchanged; mathematical and coding domains are only discussed.

E2.justification: The original matched-training comparators are retained. v3 adds random inference-only delegation and two i-LaCy variants, plus reported comparisons with GPT2, Llama 2-7B, Llama 3.1-8B and LMLM with and without database retrieval. Table 7 explicitly attributes several scores to prior work; database-based LMLM is distinct from the retained LLM-judge annotation baseline.

E3.justification: New protocols retrain methods with 10% training-time calls, sweep inference-time call budgets, and compare inference-only routing at approximately 22% calls, including a random control with probability 0.22. Appendix C adds precision, recall and F1 evaluation against author annotations on two randomly selected documents. These substantially extend the evaluation design while retaining the original main protocols.

E4.justification: v1 already includes component ablations, RAG experiments and equal-training-step comparisons. v3 adds annotation-quality auditing with complete annotated examples, training and inference call-rate sensitivity tests, and controls testing whether delegation must be learned during pretraining. These address additional questions about annotation reliability, budget dependence and the source of LaCy's benefit.

E5.justification: There are no added repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence-interval procedures or significance tests. The new entropy and log-probability scores govern i-LaCy's routing; they do not quantify uncertainty in the reported experimental results.

E6.justification: Substantial new results accompany the added analyses. Table 6 reports spaCy annotation F1 scores of 75.9% and 74.7%, versus LMLM's 46.1% and 66.5%. Figures 15–16 report LaCy FactScores of 20.48% and 22.22% with 10% training calls, and Tables 8–9 add call-budget and inference-only outcomes. The original headline LaCy scores, 22.71% and 22.03%, remain unchanged.

T1.justification: The acceptability definition, LaCy call mask, training objectives and Appendix A loss definitions are retained. The added conceptual discussion and routing heuristics introduce no substantive formal assumptions, theoretical derivations or proofs.

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction now explicitly locate the demonstrated spaCy benefits in Wikipedia-like domains and emphasize the need for domain-specific signals. This qualifies the scope of the contribution while retaining the central claims about loss insufficiency and improved factual delegation.

C2.justification: Section 3 and new Appendix D explain why localized Wikipedia facts support token-level delegation and why mathematical reasoning or code may require different signals. Appendix C discusses annotation utility beyond agreement with human labels. Appendix E adds explanations for pretraining-time delegation's advantage, practical uses of i-LaCy, and explicit training-budget and retrieval caveats for comparisons with LMLM.

D1.justification: v3 documents i-LaCy's online annotation, top-20 entropy calculation, routing calibration and random-control probability, and supplies complete human, spaCy and LMLM annotation examples. Section 5.1 refines the training-token budget description. The existing architecture, hardware, optimizer, preprocessing and hyperparameter details in Appendix A are essentially unchanged.

R1.justification: Section 2.2 adds comparisons with mixed cross-entropy, concept-aware models and speculative decoding. References are also added for data-constrained scaling and the newly compared Llama models. These locally expand the positioning while retaining the existing relationship to loss-based selection, LLM-judge annotation and model cascades.

P1.justification: The abstract and parts of the introduction are rewritten, explanatory paragraphs are added, and appendix results are reorganized from C into E with a separate NLU subsection. The main section sequence and most existing methodological and experimental prose remain intact.

P2.justification: v3 substantially expands the appendix displays with four new tables, two call-rate result figures and six color-coded annotation examples. Existing displays are largely retained and repositioned: for example, v1's equal-step Figure 10 becomes Figure 14, and its NLU Table 6 becomes Table 10. These are additions and relocations rather than replacements of the original evidence.

improvement.justification: The call-budget tests and inference-only controls strengthen support for LaCy's training-time design, while the domain qualifications and LMLM comparison caveats clarify its applicability. The gains remain limited: the annotation audit covers only two documents, uncertainty reporting is unchanged, and some new prose overgeneralizes. For example, the claim that 10% training calls lower factual accuracy does not fit 1.3B LaCy's 22.22% versus 22.03% at 15%. Overall, v3 provides useful additional validation without fundamentally changing the established evidence.
